each chaeta with apical, dynamic microvilli (Fig. 2.1d) (O’Clair
and Cloney, 1974). This formation mechanism results in the
characteristic chaetal ultrastructure with bundles of parallel lon-
gitudinal canals, the walls of which are the polymerized chitin.
Even though the basic principles of chaetal formation are in all
cases similar, the cellular machinery of chaetogenesis is high-
ly plastic and allows the construction of the plethora of chaetal
types (Tlic, et al., 2015a; Tilic et al., 2016; Tilic et al., 2017; Tilic
etal., 2019b; Tilic et al., 2021a) (Fig. 2.4).

The major external body features of Annelida are described here,
though some, such as branchiae, sensory organs, and reproduc-
tive organs, are dealt with in other sections.

The ‘head’ is composed of the prostomium, peristomium, and,
in some cases, anterior segments (Fig. 2.2). The prostomium
contains at least part of the brain, and often has eyes, antennae,
and palps. Prostomia vary a great deal in shape from conical
or semi-spherical, T-shaped structures, to elongate lobes that
extend back along the body. In some cases, the prostomium
may appear to be composed of two elements owing to a fissure
line. In other taxa, the prostomium is transformed into a mass of
palps or a radiolar crown and is hardly identifiable as a separate
structure (Figs. 2.2c, h). In many cases the prostomium may be
fused to the peristomium (Figs. 2.2a, i, k). In some cases, such

as Maldanidae and Paraonidae, the joint structure is well separat-
ed from the rest of the body as a distinct head. In taxa such as
Paraonidae, Phyllodocida, and Amphinomida, the only adult peris-
tomial structure visible is the area immediately surrounding the
mouth, and so the head is essentially prostomial, except where
segments are incorporated into the head (most Phyllodocida, see
below). In many taxa the peristomium is one (e.g. Arenicolidae,
Cossura, Scalibregmatidae, Sabellidae), or two (e.g. Eunicidae) com-
plete rings separating the prostomium from the first segment
(Figs. 2.2b, c, d, e, f, j). In taxa such as Acrocirridae and Spionidae,
the peristomium may be difficult to see dorsally, but still appears
to form a ring (Fig. 2.2d). Rouse and Fauchald (1997) scored
many annelid groups as having limited peristomium, as seen in
Phyllodocida. While this is still accepted here for taxa such as Phyl-
lodocida and Amphinomida, this interpretation has been revised
for many other taxa following Rouse and Pleijel (2001).

Head appendages include antennae, palps, peristomial cirri, and,
associated with one or more cephalized segments, anterior dor-
sal cirri. Antennae are always located on the prostomium. Up to
three antennae may be present, including a pair of lateral anten-
nae and one median antenna (Figs. 2.2a, b, i, k). Most common
are simple, tapering or digitiform antennae (e.g. Amphinomi-
dae, Hesionidae), though they may be articulated (e.g, Eunicidae),
or consist of a basal ceratophore and a distal ceratostyle (e.g.
Polynoidae). The lateral antennae may be located at or near the
frontal edge of the prostomium (e.g. Hesionidae). In some cases,
the lateral antennae are missing, leaving a single median anten-
na (e.g. Aphroditidae). Some non-Aciculata taxa, such as some
